hypotheses.title: onlyOperator modifier uses OR instead of AND, allowing any operator to bypass owner check
hypotheses.description: The modifier `if (msg.sender != owner() || operator[msg.sender]) revert ErrInvalidOperator();` reverts only when the caller is NOT the owner OR is an operator. This means the check passes (does not revert) only when the caller IS the owner AND is NOT an operator. Any address granted operator status via `updateOperator` will be permanently blocked, while the owner (if also an operator) is blocked too. More critically, the logic is inverted: the intended semantics (owner OR operator allowed) is broken, so legitimate operators cannot call harvest/delegate/finalise functions, and the owner can only call them if not marked as operator.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner calls `updateOperator(alice, true)`. 2. Alice (trusted operator) attempts `harvest(...)` — the modifier evaluates `alice != owner() || operator[alice]` = `true || true` = true → reverts. 3. Conversely, if owner is also set as operator, owner is locked out. The intended privileged set is misconfigured, potentially leaving critical functions (finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch, delegateAmount) uncallable, or if owner is the only caller, operators are useless.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on all operator-gated functions (harvest, delegate, redelegate, undelegate, finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch). Withdrawal epochs can never be finalised, freezing user funds indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change to `if (msg.sender != owner() && !operator[msg.sender]) revert ErrInvalidOperator();`.

hypotheses.title: onlyOperator modifier logic is inverted, allowing any non-owner to operate
hypotheses.description: The modifier is written as `if (msg.sender != owner() || operator[msg.sender]) revert ErrInvalidOperator();`. This reverts when the caller is the owner OR when the caller is a registered operator — i.e., it only allows callers who are neither the owner nor an operator. Any untrusted external actor who is not the owner and not an operator passes the check. This inverts the intended access control on all operator-gated functions (`harvest`, `harvestAndDelegateRewards`, `delegateAmount`, `redelegateAmount`, `undelegateAmount`, `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch`).
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` (or `harvest`, `delegateAmount`, etc.) directly. Because they are not the owner and not an operator, the modifier does not revert, and the function executes with full operator privileges.
hypotheses.impact: Anyone can finalise epochs, harvest, delegate, redelegate, and undelegate — draining rewards, manipulating epoch finalisation, and locking user shares. Complete loss of operator-only invariants.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the condition to `if (msg.sender != owner() && !operator[msg.sender]) revert ErrInvalidOperator();`.

hypotheses.title: redeem(uint256) uses current withdrawalEpoch in event instead of requested epoch
hypotheses.description: In `redeem(uint256 _epoch)`, the local variable `epoch` is set to `withdrawalEpoch` (the current, possibly advanced epoch) rather than `_epoch`. The `WithdrawalClaimed` event therefore emits the wrong epoch. While not directly exploitable for fund loss, it corrupts off-chain accounting and indexers tracking user claims per epoch.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user requests withdrawal in epoch 5. Owner finalises epoch 5, incrementing `withdrawalEpoch` to 6. User calls `redeem(5)`. The event emits `epoch = 6` instead of 5, misleading any off-chain system relying on the event to reconcile claims.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect event data; off-chain indexers/UI may misattribute claims, causing accounting confusion but no direct on-chain fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Emit `_epoch` in the `WithdrawalClaimed` event instead of `epoch`.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor inflation attack via direct WRON donation to vault
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` includes `super.totalAssets()` which is `IERC20(asset()).balanceOf(address(this))`. An attacker can deposit 1 wei (getting 1 share), then transfer WRON directly to the vault address, inflating the share price. The next depositor's shares are rounded down to zero, and the attacker redeems the victim's deposit. The `_decimalsOffset()` is not overridden (defaults to 0), so no virtual-share protection exists.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `deposit(1)` to mint 1 share. 2) Attacker transfers a large amount of WRON directly to the vault via `IERC20(wron).transfer(vault, X)`. 3) Victim calls `deposit(Y)` where Y < X; `previewDeposit` computes shares = Y * totalSupply / totalAssets = Y * 1 / (1+X) = 0. 4) Attacker redeems 1 share for X+Y assets.
hypotheses.impact: Victim loses their entire deposit; attacker steals it. Direct loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Override `_decimalsOffset()` to return a non-zero value (e.g. 3-6) or use virtual shares/assets, and/or track assets internally rather than relying on `balanceOf`.

hypotheses.title: Pause traps users' pending withdrawal requests indefinitely
hypotheses.description: `redeem(uint256 _epoch)` is gated by `whenNotPaused`, so once the owner pauses the contract, users who already requested withdrawals cannot claim their finalized RON. The `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` is also `whenNotPaused`, so even the finalization step is blocked. Funds sit in escrow with no user-callable path to retrieve them while paused.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Users call `requestWithdrawal()` and shares are locked. 2) Owner (or compromised owner key) calls `pause()`. 3) `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` and `redeem(uint256)` both revert with `ErrPaused`. 4) Users cannot retrieve their RON until unpause, which may never happen.
hypotheses.impact: User funds permanently frozen in escrow; no recovery path exists for users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow `redeem(uint256)` and `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` to run even when paused, or add an emergency withdrawal path that bypasses the pause.

hypotheses.title: finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch can be called repeatedly, re-locking shares and draining escrow
hypotheses.description: `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` reads `lockedSharesPerEpoch[epoch]`, sets `statusPerEpoch[epoch] = FINALISED`, increments `withdrawalEpoch`, and transfers `assets` from the vault to `escrow`. It does not check whether the epoch was already finalised, and `lockedSharesPerEpoch[epoch]` is never reset. An operator (or anyone if the operator check is bypassed via the broken `onlyOperator` modifier — see separate finding) can call it again for the same epoch, re-computing `assets = previewRedeem(lockedShares)` and moving a second tranche of assets to escrow, while `lockedPricePerSharePerEpoch[epoch]` is overwritten. Users who already redeemed in that epoch have `request.fulfilled = true`, so they cannot claim again, but the escrow now holds extra assets that no one can claim, and the vault's share supply/asset backing is corrupted.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor who can satisfy `onlyOperator` (see modifier bug) calls `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` twice for the same epoch. The second call re-locks the same shares and moves additional assets to escrow. The vault's `totalAssets` drops by the duplicated amount, and the escrow balance grows without corresponding claims.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vault assets to escrow (frozen/unclaimable), incorrect share pricing for subsequent epochs, potential insolvency of the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `statusPerEpoch[epoch] == STANDBY` before finalising, and zero out `lockedSharesPerEpoch[epoch]` after finalisation.

hypotheses.title: pruneValidatorList is permissionless and can be used to grief validator tracking
hypotheses.description: `pruneValidatorList` has no access modifier, so any external actor can call it. It iterates over all validators and proxies, calling `IRoninValidator.getReward` and `getManyStakingAmounts`. If a validator has zero rewards and zero staking across all proxies, it is removed via `_removeValidator`. An attacker can call this at a moment when a validator temporarily has zero rewards/stake (e.g., just after harvest but before re-delegation) to remove it from the tracking list, even though it may still be actively used.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Operator harvests rewards from validator V, leaving V with zero rewards momentarily. 2. Attacker front-runs the next delegate call and invokes `pruneValidatorList()`. 3. V is removed from `validators` array. 4. Subsequent `getTotalStaked`/`getTotalRewards` no longer include V, under-reporting total assets. 5. If V still has stake, `totalAssets()` is wrong, affecting share pricing.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect `totalAssets()` calculation, leading to mispriced shares (deposit/redeem at wrong ratio), potential loss for users and protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `pruneValidatorList` to `onlyOperator` or `onlyOwner`, or require that the validator has been inactive for a sustained period.

hypotheses.title: operatorFeeAmount not deducted from totalAssets, causing share price overstatement
hypotheses.description: `harvest` adds `(harvestedAmount * operatorFee) / BIPS` to `operatorFeeAmount`, but `getTotalRewards()` already subtracts the fee from rewards before adding to `totalAssets`. The harvested amount is deposited into the vault as WRON (increasing `super.totalAssets()`), yet the fee portion is still owed to `feeRecipient` and is not subtracted from `totalAssets`. So `totalAssets` overstates real holdings by `operatorFeeAmount` until `fetchOperatorFee` is called.
hypotheses.attackPath: After a harvest, an attacker deposits and immediately redeems; the share price includes the un-withdrawn fee, so the attacker captures a portion of the fee that belongs to the fee recipient. Repeated harvests amplify the leak.
hypotheses.impact: Fee recipient loses fees; depositors/withdrawers get mispriced shares. Insolvency risk if fee is large.
hypotheses.recommendation: Subtract `operatorFeeAmount` from `totalAssets()` (or from `super.totalAssets()`) so the fee is not counted as depositor-owned assets.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in withdraw/redeem via native RON callback after share burn
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` calls `super.withdraw(_assets, address(this), _owner)` which burns shares and transfers WRON to the vault, then calls `_withdrawRONTo(_receiver, _assets)` which sends native RON via low-level `call`. The receiver's fallback can reenter `withdraw`, `redeem`, `deposit`, or `requestWithdrawal`. Since `totalAssets()` depends on live staking/reward queries and the vault's WRON balance, a reentrant call can observe inconsistent state (e.g., shares burned but assets not yet sent, or vice versa) and mint/redeem at manipulated prices.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `withdraw(assets, attackerContract, attacker)` where attackerContract's `receive()` reenters `deposit()` or `mint()` to mint shares at a price that doesn't reflect the pending withdrawal. 2) Alternatively, reenter `redeem` to burn shares at a stale exchange rate. 3) Profit from the price discrepancy.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of funds from the vault, incorrect share minting/burning, insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` modifier to all state-mutating external functions (`withdraw`, `redeem`, `deposit`, `mint`, `requestWithdrawal`, `redeem(uint256)`, `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch`).

hypotheses.title: finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch can be called with zero locked shares, locking epoch
hypotheses.description: `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` increments `withdrawalEpoch` and marks the current epoch FINALISED even if `lockedSharesPerEpoch[epoch] == 0`. Because the modifier is broken (see other finding), any untrusted actor can call this repeatedly, advancing `withdrawalEpoch` and finalising empty epochs. Users who later call `requestWithdrawal` will be placed in a new epoch, but any user who requested in the skipped epoch will have their shares locked with `lockedPricePerSharePerEpoch` set to (0,0), making `_convertToAssets` divide by zero or return 0.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` repeatedly to advance `withdrawalEpoch`. Users who requested withdrawal in an epoch that gets finalised with zero shares (or before they can claim) have their shares transferred to the contract but `lockedPricePerSharePerEpoch` records (0,0). When they call `redeem(_epoch)`, `_convertToAssets(shares, 0, 0)` computes `shares * 1 / (0 + 10**offset)` which may return 0, so they receive nothing while their shares are burned.
hypotheses.impact: Users lose their staked RON/shares permanently; funds effectively frozen or stolen by the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `lockedShares > 0` before finalising, or handle zero-share epochs by not advancing state; also fix the `onlyOperator` modifier.

hypotheses.title: Withdrawal requests can be redeemed in later epochs at inflated share price
hypotheses.description: `redeem(uint256 _epoch)` accepts any finalized epoch and converts shares using that epoch's locked price-per-share, without requiring the user to redeem in the epoch they requested. A user can request a withdrawal in epoch N, wait for a later epoch M where the price-per-share has increased (due to accumulated rewards still counted in that later lock), and redeem in epoch M using the higher price. Worse, the user's shares remain locked in `withdrawalRequestsPerEpoch[N]` while also being convertible in epoch M, so the same economic exposure keeps accruing reward value across many epochs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls `requestWithdrawal(shares)` in epoch N. 2) User does not redeem immediately. 3) Operator finalises later epochs N+1, N+2, ... whose locked per-share price grows as more rewards are harvested. 4) User calls `redeem(_epoch=N+k)` for a much later epoch, receiving the higher asset amount for the shares that were locked at epoch N. 5) Since `request.fulfilled` is per-epoch-per-user, the user can also split requests across epochs and claim from multiple favorable locks.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting: user extracts more assets than the epoch-N lock intended, draining the escrow's asset buffer and potentially leaving later redeemers insolvent (bad debt).
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_epoch == withdrawalEpoch - 1` (or track per-user the exact epoch they requested) so the locked price-per-share used corresponds to the epoch the shares were locked in.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal lacks check that _shares > 0, allowing zero-share spam and event pollution
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` does not validate `_shares > 0`. A user can call it with zero shares, creating a `WithdrawalRequest` entry and emitting `WithdrawalRequested` with zero amount. This pollutes state and events, and combined with `_checkUserCanReceiveRon` performing an external call, allows cheap griefing/spam.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker repeatedly calls `requestWithdrawal(0)` from many addresses, bloating `withdrawalRequestsPerEpoch` mappings and emitting spurious events. No funds lost but state/event noise increases and gas costs for legitimate users may rise if any iteration over requests is added later.
hypotheses.impact: State bloat and event spam; no direct fund loss but degrades protocol hygiene and could complicate future logic that iterates requests.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(_shares > 0, "LiquidRon: zero shares");` at the start of `requestWithdrawal`.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal shares not burned, allowing double-spend via redeem
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` transfers shares to the vault (`_transfer(msg.sender, address(this), _shares)`) but does not burn them. The vault holds these shares and they remain in `totalSupply`. When `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` runs, `previewRedeem(lockedShares)` is computed against the full supply including the locked shares, and `_withdraw` burns them from the vault. However, between `requestWithdrawal` and `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch`, the vault's own shares are counted in `totalSupply`, so `previewRedeem`/`previewWithdraw` for other users is diluted. More critically, the vault-held shares can be moved by anyone who can call `_withdraw` on the vault's behalf — but the real issue is that `lockedSharesPerEpoch` is added on top of shares still in circulation, so `totalAssets`/`totalSupply` accounting is inconsistent during the epoch.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user requests withdrawal of X shares; those shares sit in the vault. Another user can call `redeem`/`withdraw` and the share price is computed including the locked shares, giving them a favorable rate. Then at finalisation, `previewRedeem(lockedShares)` uses the same inflated supply, so the locked user receives fewer assets than expected.
hypotheses.impact: Withdrawing users receive less than fair value; remaining holders benefit at their expense. Accounting drift between epochs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Burn the shares in `requestWithdrawal` (or exclude vault-held locked shares from `totalSupply` used in pricing) so that locked shares do not affect the price for other users.

hypotheses.title: totalAssets() uses manipulable spot rewards from validator contract
hypotheses.description: totalAssets() is computed as super.totalAssets() + getTotalStaked() + getTotalRewards(), where getTotalRewards() reads live reward balances from the Ronin validator contract via getRewards/getManyStakingAmounts. These values are not snapshotted and can change between the moment a user submits a deposit/mint transaction and the moment it executes, and they can be influenced by anyone who can trigger reward accrual (e.g., by calling harvest or by staking/unstaking activity). Because ERC4626 deposit/mint/withdraw/redeem all derive share prices from totalAssets(), a user can sandwich their own deposit around a reward-accrual event to mint shares at an artificially low price or redeem at an artificially high price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes pending reward accrual (or triggers it via a public harvest path / validator activity). 2) Attacker front-runs the accrual with a large deposit()/mint() when totalAssets() is low, receiving more shares than fair. 3) Reward accrual lands, totalAssets() jumps. 4) Attacker redeems/withdraws immediately, extracting the delta from other LPs.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution of existing depositors and direct value extraction from the vault; wrong share accounting on every deposit/redeem that lands near a reward update.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot reward/stake values at epoch boundaries (as done for withdrawals) and use the snapshot for share pricing, or require deposits/redeems to use a previously committed price-per-share rather than live validator reads.

hypotheses.title: finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch uses live previewRedeem for locked price
hypotheses.description: The locked price per share for a withdrawal epoch is set from previewRedeem(lockedShares) evaluated at the moment the operator calls finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch(). previewRedeem depends on totalAssets(), which includes live getTotalRewards()/getTotalStaked() reads from the validator contract. An untrusted actor can influence these live values (e.g., by triggering reward accrual, staking/unstaking, or by depositing/redeeming right before finalisation) so that the locked price is skewed in their favour for the epoch they have a pending withdrawal in.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker requests a withdrawal in epoch N. 2) Attacker manipulates totalAssets() (e.g., triggers reward accrual or a large deposit/redeem) right before the operator's finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch() transaction lands. 3) The lockedPricePerSharePerEpoch[N] is recorded at the manipulated price. 4) Attacker calls redeem(N) and receives more assets than fair, draining the escrow.
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment to withdrawing users, under-collateralisation of remaining shares, potential insolvency of the vault for later redeemers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the locked price from a snapshot of totalAssets taken at request time or at a deterministic epoch boundary, not from a live previewRedeem at finalisation.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in redeem(epoch) via native RON callback before state finalization
hypotheses.description: In `redeem(uint256 _epoch)`, the function sets `request.fulfilled = true` before the external calls, but the `_withdrawRONTo(msg.sender, assets)` sends native RON to the caller via a low-level `call`, which can reenter. However, the more critical issue is that `IERC20(asset()).transferFrom(escrow, address(this), assets)` is called before `_withdrawRONTo`, and the escrow's WRON transfer is a standard ERC20 transfer. The reentrancy risk here is that the attacker can reenter `redeem` for a different epoch, or reenter `requestWithdrawal`/`deposit` while the vault's accounting is mid-update. Since `request.fulfilled` is set before the external call, direct reentrancy on the same epoch is blocked, but cross-epoch and cross-function reentrancy remains possible because `withdrawalEpoch` and other state are not snapshotted.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker requests withdrawal in epoch N and epoch N+1. 2) Operator finalizes both epochs. 3) Attacker calls `redeem(N)`; during `_withdrawRONTo`, the attacker's `receive()` reenters `redeem(N+1)` or `deposit()`/`requestWithdrawal()`, manipulating share/asset accounting while the first call's state is partially updated. 4) Attacker can also reenter `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` if they are an operator (not untrusted) — but as untrusted, they can reenter `deposit()` to mint shares at stale price.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share/asset accounting, potential theft of funds from other users' locked withdrawals, or inflation of shares.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply a nonReentrant guard on `redeem(uint256)`, `withdraw`, `redeem(uint256,address,address)`, `deposit`, `mint`, and `requestWithdrawal`, or use a checks-effects-interactions pattern with a reentrancy lock.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in requestWithdrawal via _checkUserCanReceiveRon callback
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` calls `_checkUserCanReceiveRon(msg.sender)` which performs a low-level `call{value: 0}` to the user. This call can trigger the user's fallback/receive function, allowing reentrancy before the state updates (`request.shares += _shares`, `lockedSharesPerEpoch[epoch] += _shares`, `_transfer`). An attacker can reenter `requestWithdrawal` or other functions to manipulate the locked shares or share balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `requestWithdrawal(shares)` from a contract whose `receive()` reenters `requestWithdrawal` with more shares or `deposit()` to mint shares. 2) Since the state updates happen after the external call, the attacker can double-count shares or manipulate the locked shares per epoch.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect locked shares accounting, potential theft of funds from the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `_checkUserCanReceiveRon` after the state updates, or add a `nonReentrant` modifier to `requestWithdrawal`.

hypotheses.title: pruneValidatorList unbounded loop over validators and proxies
hypotheses.description: `pruneValidatorList` iterates over `validatorCount` and for each validator loops over all `stakingProxyCount` proxies, calling `getReward` and `getManyStakingAmounts` on the Ronin staking contract. As validators and proxies grow, this becomes prohibitively expensive and will revert out-of-gas, making pruning impossible. Since `_tryPushValidator` only adds and never removes without pruning, the validator list can grow unboundedly.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator (or any caller of `harvestAndDelegateRewards`/`delegateAmount`/`redelegateAmount`) can push many new validators via `_tryPushValidator`. Over time `validatorCount` grows, and `pruneValidatorList` becomes uncallable due to gas limits, so stale validators remain in `validators` and are iterated in `getTotalStaked`/`getTotalRewards`, inflating gas for all view calls and potentially breaking `totalAssets()`.
hypotheses.impact: `totalAssets()` and related views become uncallable (out-of-gas), breaking deposits/withdrawals that depend on them; validator list cannot be cleaned.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make pruning incremental (bounded batch size) or track per-validator activity to avoid full scans.

hypotheses.title: redeem(epoch) does not verify caller has a request; zero-share claim drains escrow
hypotheses.description: `redeem(uint256 _epoch)` reads `withdrawalRequestsPerEpoch[_epoch][msg.sender]` and only checks `request.fulfilled` and `statusPerEpoch[_epoch] == FINALISED`. It never checks that `request.shares > 0`. If a user has no request in that epoch, `shares = 0`, `assets = _convertToAssets(0, ...) = 0`, and the function still sets `request.fulfilled = true` and calls `IERC20(asset()).transferFrom(escrow, address(this), 0)` and `_withdrawRONTo(msg.sender, 0)`. While the immediate transfer is zero, this marks the request as fulfilled and, combined with the missing reset of `request.shares`, can be used to grief or to pre-empt a legitimate later claim if the user later acquires shares in the same epoch (the fulfilled flag blocks them).
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls `redeem(_epoch)` for an epoch where they have no request. The call succeeds, setting `fulfilled = true`. If the user later receives shares in that same epoch (e.g., via a transfer from another user who requested), they can no longer claim because `fulfilled` is already true.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / denial of claim for users who receive shares in an epoch after calling `redeem` with zero shares; no direct fund loss but frozen claim rights.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `request.shares > 0` before processing the claim, and reset `request.shares = 0` after a successful redeem.

hypotheses.title: Front-running finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch to manipulate locked price per share
hypotheses.description: `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch()` locks the price per share for the current epoch by calling `previewRedeem(lockedShares)`. An attacker can front-run this transaction by depositing a large amount of RON or requesting a withdrawal to manipulate `totalAssets()` and thus the locked price per share. Since `totalAssets()` includes live staking rewards and staked amounts, an attacker can also trigger a harvest or delegate/undelegate to change the total assets right before finalization, affecting the locked price for all users in that epoch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes the operator's `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` transaction in the mempool. 2) Attacker front-runs by depositing a large amount of RON (increasing totalAssets) or by calling `harvest` (if operator) to inflate rewards. 3) The locked price per share is now higher/lower than it should be, benefiting the attacker when they redeem their shares in that epoch.
hypotheses.impact: The attacker can manipulate the locked price per share to their advantage, causing other users to receive fewer assets or the vault to become insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a commit-reveal scheme or a time-weighted average price for finalization, or restrict deposits/withdrawals during the finalization block.

hypotheses.title: Escrow.deposit is callable by vault only, but vault's deposit() is payable and re-entrant via Escrow
hypotheses.description: `Escrow.deposit` checks `msg.sender == _vault` and then calls `IVault(_vault).deposit{value: _amount}(_amount, _receiver)`. The vault's `deposit()` is `external payable` and calls `_depositRONTo(escrow, msg.value)` then `Escrow(escrow).deposit(msg.value, msg.sender)`. Because the vault sends WRON to escrow before calling escrow.deposit, and escrow then calls back into vault.deposit (which is payable but receives no value in this path), the flow is convoluted. An attacker cannot directly call Escrow.deposit (not vault), but the vault's `receive()` also calls `_depositRONTo(escrow, msg.value)` and `Escrow(escrow).deposit(msg.value, msg.sender)` — meaning any direct RON transfer to the vault triggers escrow.deposit which calls vault.deposit (payable, msg.value=0) which again calls escrow.deposit... This is a reentrancy loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker sends 1 wei RON directly to LiquidRon via `selfdestruct` or plain transfer. `receive()` fires: `_depositRONTo(escrow, 1)` then `Escrow(escrow).deposit(1, attacker)`. Escrow calls `IVault(vault).deposit{value:1}(1, attacker)` — but vault has no RON (it was sent to escrow), so this call has msg.value=0 and vault.deposit() runs `_depositRONTo(escrow, 0)` then `Escrow(escrow).deposit(0, attacker)` → infinite recursion / out-of-gas, or at minimum unexpected state.
hypotheses.impact: Potential out-of-gas DoS on direct RON transfers to the vault; unexpected share minting or accounting corruption if recursion terminates.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `receive()`, do not call `Escrow.deposit`; instead directly credit shares or use a non-reentrant guard. Add `nonReentrant` to `deposit()` and `receive()`.

hypotheses.title: finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch uses previewRedeem which can revert or misprice on empty epoch
hypotheses.description: If `lockedShares == 0` (no withdrawal requests in the epoch), `previewRedeem(0)` returns 0 and `_withdraw` is called with 0 assets and 0 shares. `_burn(owner, 0)` is fine, but `lockedPricePerSharePerEpoch[epoch]` is set to (0,0). Later, if a user somehow has a request in that epoch (impossible since lockedShares is 0), `_convertToAssets` divides by `_totalShares + 10**_decimalsOffset()` = 1, which is safe. However, if `lockedShares > 0` but `previewRedeem` rounds down to 0 assets (dust shares), the user receives 0 assets for their shares and the shares are burned — permanent loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user requests withdrawal of a tiny share amount such that `previewRedeem(shares)` rounds to 0. At finalisation, their shares are burned and they receive 0 assets. Their funds are effectively donated to remaining holders.
hypotheses.impact: Dust-share withdrawers lose their shares for zero assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `assets > 0` in `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` or in `requestWithdrawal` (reject dust requests), or round up in favor of the withdrawer.

hypotheses.title: redeem(epoch) uses stale locked price without freshness check
hypotheses.description: redeem(uint256 _epoch) reads lockedPricePerSharePerEpoch[_epoch] and converts shares to assets using that stored ratio, with no check that the epoch is recent or that the stored ratio still reflects the vault's current solvency. If the vault's real assets have declined (e.g., slashing, undelegation losses, or operator fee changes) after finalisation, the stored ratio over-pays redeemers relative to the vault's actual backing, and the escrow may be drained faster than assets are replenished.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker requests withdrawal in epoch N. 2) After finalisation, vault assets decline (slashing / losses / fee change). 3) Attacker calls redeem(N) and receives assets at the old, higher locked price, taking more than their fair share of the now-smaller pool.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency for later redeemers; loss of funds for remaining shareholders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap redemption payout at the current previewRedeem value, or re-validate the locked price against current totalAssets before paying out.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal accepts shares without minimum-out or price check
hypotheses.description: requestWithdrawal(uint256 _shares) locks the user's shares into the current epoch with no parameter for a minimum acceptable assets amount and no check on the current price-per-share. The eventual payout is determined later by finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch() using a live previewRedeem, so the user has no on-chain guarantee about the price at which their shares will be redeemed. An untrusted actor who can influence totalAssets() (see related findings) can move the price against the requester between request and finalisation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim calls requestWithdrawal(shares). 2) Attacker manipulates totalAssets() downward (e.g., by triggering a large redeem or by timing around reward accrual) before finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch(). 3) The locked price is set low, and the victim receives fewer assets than expected on redeem(epoch).
hypotheses.impact: Victim receives less than fair value; value transferred to the attacker or to other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a minAssetsOut parameter to requestWithdrawal and enforce it at redeem(epoch), or snapshot the price at request time.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in totalAssets via staking proxy callbacks
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` calls `getTotalStaked()` and `getTotalRewards()`, which make external calls to `IRoninValidator(roninStaking).getManyStakingAmounts` and `getRewards`. If the Ronin staking contract or any proxy makes an external call back into the vault (e.g., via a malicious validator or a callback), the vault's `totalAssets()` can return a manipulated value during the callback. An attacker can exploit this by triggering a callback during a deposit/withdraw and reading `totalAssets()` in a reentrant context to compute an incorrect share price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious contract that interacts with the vault. 2) During a `deposit` or `withdraw`, the attacker triggers a callback (e.g., via a malicious validator address in `_consensusAddrs`) that reenters a view function like `previewDeposit` or `convertToShares`. 3) The view function reads `totalAssets()` which is mid-update, leading to incorrect share calculations.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect share pricing, potential theft of funds via arbitrage.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a reentrancy guard on all external functions and ensure view functions used in pricing are not callable during state transitions, or cache `totalAssets()` before external calls.

hypotheses.title: _checkUserCanReceiveRon griefable via reverting receiver
hypotheses.description: `_checkUserCanReceiveRon` performs `payable(_user).call{value: 0}("")` and reverts if it fails. A user whose address is a contract that reverts on receive (or a smart wallet with restrictive fallback) can never call `requestWithdrawal`, but more importantly, if a user's address later becomes unable to receive (e.g., self-destructed or upgraded), their already-requested withdrawal in `redeem(uint256)` will also fail because `_withdrawRONTo` uses a plain `call` and reverts on failure.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User requests withdrawal from a contract address. 2) Later the contract's receive function is changed to revert (or the contract is a multisig with a failing fallback). 3) `redeem(uint256)` calls `_withdrawRONTo(msg.sender, assets)` which reverts, permanently locking that user's claim.
hypotheses.impact: Individual user's finalized withdrawal becomes unclaimable; funds stuck in escrow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow the user to specify an alternate receiver address in `redeem(uint256)`, or use a pull-based claim pattern.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal lacks per-epoch nonce/deadline; replay of stale requests across epochs
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` accumulates shares into `withdrawalRequestsPerEpoch[withdrawalEpoch][msg.sender]` with no per-request nonce, deadline, or chain-id binding. A user's signed intent (if any meta-transaction or off-chain signed request is used by integrators) is not bound to a specific epoch, so the same authorization can be replayed in a later epoch, or a stale request can be re-submitted after the user intended to cancel. The contract also never clears `request.shares` after a successful `redeem`, so a user who requested in epoch N and claimed can still have the shares counted if the same epoch is somehow re-finalised or if accounting is reused.
hypotheses.attackPath: An integrator or relayer that accepts signed withdrawal intents can be tricked into replaying a user's signed request in a subsequent epoch (no epoch/nonce in the signed payload), causing the user's shares to be locked again without fresh consent. Alternatively, a user who claimed in epoch N retains `request.shares` in storage; if any logic re-reads it (e.g., a future migration or a re-finalisation path), the same shares can be claimed twice.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized locking of user shares; potential double-claim of assets from escrow if the stale `request.shares` is ever re-processed, leading to escrow insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `withdrawalEpoch`, a per-user nonce, `block.chainid`, and `address(this)` in any signed withdrawal intent, and zero out `request.shares` after a successful `redeem`.

hypotheses.title: `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` locks price-per-share while rewards remain uncollected, enabling dilution/skew
hypotheses.description: `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` snapshots `previewRedeem(lockedShares)` as the locked price-per-share for the epoch. `previewRedeem` depends on `totalAssets()`, which includes `getTotalRewards()` from staking proxies. Because harvested rewards are shared pro-rata with all outstanding shares, while locked shares from previous epochs have not yet been burned, the locked ratio is computed against a total share supply that still includes shares already committed for withdrawal. This lets the operator-triggered snapshot (which any user can influence by depositing/withdrawing just before finalisation) be skewed in favor of requesters at the expense of remaining holders.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An untrusted user observes pending harvest or reward accrual. 2) Immediately before `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch`, they `requestWithdrawal` for a large share amount. 3) When the epoch is finalised, `previewRedeem(lockedShares)` uses the enlarged asset base (including unclaimed rewards that will later be harvested). 4) The locked price per share is inflated relative to the eventual realised assets, and the requester redeems at that inflated price, leaving remaining stakers with diluted value.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair distribution: later remaining holders bear the shortfall from the over-valuation of locked shares, effectively paying the withdrawing user out of future rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the locked price-per-share from realised assets only (exclude `getTotalRewards()` accrual), or require rewards to be harvested before snapshot; alternatively burn locked shares into a virtual supply at lock time.

hypotheses.title: fetchOperatorFee can be called by feeRecipient even when paused, and feeRecipient can be set to any address by owner
hypotheses.description: `fetchOperatorFee` has no `whenNotPaused` modifier and only checks `msg.sender == feeRecipient`. If `feeRecipient` is set to a contract that can be triggered by an untrusted party (e.g., a public function that calls fetchOperatorFee), the fee can be drained during a pause. More importantly, the function lacks a pause check, so fee withdrawal is possible even when the protocol is paused for emergencies.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner sets `feeRecipient` to a contract with a public `claim()` that calls `LiquidRon.fetchOperatorFee()`. During a pause (e.g., due to a discovered bug), any user calls `claim()` on the feeRecipient contract, draining accumulated operator fees despite the pause.
hypotheses.impact: Operator fees can be withdrawn during an emergency pause, potentially removing funds that should be frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `whenNotPaused` to `fetchOperatorFee`.

hypotheses.title: _convertToAssets rounding favors vault, but redeem(epoch) can underpay users
hypotheses.description: `_convertToAssets` uses `Math.Rounding.Floor`, which rounds down the assets paid to the withdrawing user. Combined with the `+1` / `+10**_decimalsOffset()` virtual offset, this is generally safe, but for large `_totalShares` and small `_shares`, the floor can shave meaningful value. Since the locked price is fixed at finalisation, the rounding loss is permanent for that user.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user with a small share of a large epoch receives slightly less than fair value; the difference stays in the escrow/vault and benefits remaining holders.
hypotheses.impact: Minor value leakage from withdrawers to remaining holders; not exploitable for profit by an attacker directly.
hypotheses.recommendation: Acceptable as-is for protocol-favoring rounding, but document the dust loss; consider a minimum-share threshold.

hypotheses.title: operatorFee change retroactively alters getTotalRewards and share price
hypotheses.description: getTotalRewards() subtracts (totalRewards * operatorFee) / BIPS using the current operatorFee, and totalAssets() includes this value. The owner can change operatorFee at any time with no timelock, and the code comment itself acknowledges this. While the owner is trusted, the effect is that any pending deposit/redeem/withdrawal-finalisation transaction can be front-run by an operatorFee change, changing the effective share price for that transaction. This is a price-oracle-style manipulation of the vault's share price via a parameter that is not snapshotted.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a large pending deposit or withdrawal-finalisation. 2) Attacker (or colluding owner) changes operatorFee to shift totalAssets() in the favourable direction. 3) The pending transaction executes at the manipulated price, benefiting the attacker at the expense of other users.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share pricing on affected transactions; value transfer between users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot operatorFee per epoch and use the snapshot for reward accounting, or put fee changes behind a timelock and apply them only at epoch boundaries.

hypotheses.title: _convertToAssets uses +1/+10**decimalsOffset virtual offset inconsistently with ERC4626
hypotheses.description: The custom _convertToAssets(shares, totalAssets, totalShares) computes shares * (totalAssets + 1) / (totalShares + 10**decimalsOffset). This is used in redeem(uint256 _epoch) to pay out assets from the escrow based on the locked price. Because the offset is applied to the locked totals rather than to the live totals, and because the locked totals were themselves derived from previewRedeem (which already applies the ERC4626 virtual offset), the offset is effectively applied twice. This inflates or deflates the payout relative to the true pro-rata share, and the discrepancy grows with the size of the epoch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker requests a withdrawal in an epoch with a large lockedShares value. 2) On redeem(epoch), the double-applied offset yields a payout that is systematically off from the fair pro-rata amount. 3) Attacker (or any redeemer) captures the difference at the expense of the escrow / remaining shareholders.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic mispricing of epoch redemptions; escrow drain or under-payment depending on direction.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the same conversion formula as ERC4626 (or store the already-offset price) so the offset is applied exactly once.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in deposit() via Escrow callback before share minting
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` calls `_depositRONTo(escrow, msg.value)` which deposits RON into WRON and transfers WRON to the escrow, then calls `Escrow(escrow).deposit(msg.value, msg.sender)`. The Escrow calls back into `LiquidRon.deposit(uint256,address)` which mints shares. However, the WRON transfer to the escrow and the subsequent callback can be reentered if the WRON token or the escrow has a hook. More critically, the `receive()` function also calls `_depositRONTo` and `Escrow.deposit`, and an attacker can reenter `deposit()` or `receive()` during the WRON transfer if WRON is ERC777-like. Since WRON is a standard wrapped token, the risk is lower, but the escrow callback pattern allows reentrancy if the escrow is malicious (it's not, but the pattern is fragile).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends RON to the vault via `receive()` or `deposit()`. 2) During the WRON transfer to escrow, if WRON has a hook (it doesn't in standard implementation, but the code assumes it might), the attacker reenters `deposit()` to mint shares at a stale price. 3) Alternatively, the attacker can reenter `requestWithdrawal` during the escrow callback.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect share minting, potential theft of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` modifier to `deposit()`, `receive()`, and `deposit(uint256,address)`.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal accepts zero shares and blocks nothing but wastes epoch
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` does not check `_shares > 0`, so a user can register a request with zero shares. This is harmless for the user but pollutes the epoch's `lockedSharesPerEpoch` accounting and emits misleading events. Not a strong DoS, but combined with `_checkUserCanReceiveRon` it forces a call to the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: User calls `requestWithdrawal(0)` repeatedly; each call performs an external call to `msg.sender` via `_checkUserCanReceiveRon`, which can be a contract that reverts or consumes gas.
hypotheses.impact: Minor accounting noise; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_shares > 0` in `requestWithdrawal`.

hypotheses.title: Escrow.deposit is callable by vault with arbitrary receiver, enabling share minting to attacker
hypotheses.description: `Escrow.deposit(uint256 _amount, address _receiver)` only checks `msg.sender == _vault` and then calls `IVault(_vault).deposit(_amount, _receiver)`. The vault's `deposit(uint256, address)` is `whenNotPaused` and mints shares to `_receiver` based on `_amount`. Because the vault's `deposit()` (payable) sends native RON to escrow and then calls `Escrow.deposit(msg.value, msg.sender)`, the escrow trusts the vault to pass the correct receiver. However, the vault's `receive()` also calls `_depositRONTo(escrow, msg.value)` and `Escrow(escrow).deposit(msg.value, msg.sender)` for any sender that is not the WRON token. An attacker can send native RON directly to the vault (triggering `receive()`), which forwards to escrow and then back to `vault.deposit(msg.value, attacker)`, minting shares to the attacker at the current price. This is intended for deposits, but the escrow's lack of binding between the deposited amount and the original sender means any contract that can call `Escrow.deposit` (only the vault) can mint to an arbitrary receiver — and the vault's `receive()` path lets an attacker choose themselves as receiver without going through the standard `deposit()` entrypoint.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker sends native RON to the vault address. `receive()` fires, calls `_depositRONTo(escrow, msg.value)` and `Escrow(escrow).deposit(msg.value, msg.sender)`. Escrow calls `vault.deposit(msg.value, attacker)`, minting shares to the attacker. If the attacker can manipulate `totalAssets` (e.g., via the operator-modifier bug to call `finaliseRonRewardsForEpoch` or `harvest`), they can mint shares at a favorable price.
hypotheses.impact: Share minting at manipulated prices; potential dilution of existing holders and loss of vault assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `Escrow.deposit`, bind the receiver to the original depositor (e.g., pass `msg.sender` from the vault's `receive()`/`deposit()` and verify), or remove the `receive()` shortcut and require explicit `deposit()` calls.

hypotheses.title: Undelegate deposits asset to vault then operator can re-delegate without share adjustment
hypotheses.description: `undelegateAmount` bulk-undelegates from Ronin and then `_depositRONTo(vault, totalUndelegated)`, sending WRON to the vault. On the vault side, if `_withdrawRONTo`/asset operations don't convert this into share supply changes, the vault's `totalAssets()` increases without an offsetting decrease in staked value in the validator contracts and without minting shares. The operator can then call `delegateAmount` to re-delegate, moving asset accounting between sources. There's no reconciliation between the vault's `getTotalStaked()` view (which reads validator state) and the actual token balance at each step, so balances can drift from accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator undelegates a large amount, pushing assets into the vault's WRON balance; any path that reads `totalAssets()` at that moment (e.g. `previewRedeem` when finalising an epoch, or a depositor computing shares) sees a temporary mismatch — `getTotalStaked()` may still reflect old staking or partially reflect new balances, letting a depositor who times the call mint shares at an incorrect rate.
hypotheses.impact: Depositors can be over- or under-issued shares; the vault's reported NAV diverges from realised asset backing, creating bad debt for later withdrawers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure the vault's `totalAssets()` accounting uses a consistent valuation between validator staking and vault balance, and reconcile after every delegate/undelegate via explicit accounting updates rather than derived views.

hypotheses.title: Overridden `withdraw`/`redeem` bypass ERC4626 allowance semantics on native path
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` and `redeem` pass `address(this)` as receiver to `super.withdraw`/`super.redeem`, spend allowance as the vault (not the caller), then `_withdrawRONTo(_receiver, assets)`. Any untrusted caller with a valid allowance on an owner can trigger the withdrawal and, because `_withdrawRONTo` forwards native RON with a plain call, a poorly-behaved receiver can revert the whole path — but more importantly the allowance is consumed and the vault-level `_withdraw` uses `address(this)` as `caller`, meaning the allowance is spent against the vault's balance/owner mapping, not the external caller's authority. Users could see allowance consumed by anyone calling on their behalf, then be blocked from withdrawing while paused.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker calls `withdraw(assets, attacker, victim)` where the victim has approved the vault; `_spendAllowance(owner=victim, caller=address(this), shares)` consumes victim's allowance to the vault, and assets are sent to `attacker`. Victims lose allowance and their assets can be pulled any time the vault holds enough balance.
hypotheses.impact: Approved users can be drained via the tuple-shaped allowance path without needing the caller themselves to hold victim's approval.
hypotheses.recommendation: Preserve OZ semantics by passing `msg.sender` as caller and `_receiver` as receiver through `super.withdraw`, or explicitly check allowance against `msg.sender`.

hypotheses.title: LiquidProxy.undelegateAmount deposits totalUndelegated but bulkUndelegate may return less
hypotheses.description: `undelegateAmount` sums `_amounts` into `totalUndelegated`, calls `IRoninValidator.bulkUndelegate(_consensusAddrs, _amounts)`, then `_depositRONTo(vault, totalUndelegated)`. If `bulkUndelegate` does not actually transfer the full sum (e.g., partial undelegation, slashing, or the validator contract returns less), the proxy will attempt to deposit more RON than it holds, reverting or draining other balance. Conversely, if the validator sends more, excess is stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator (or, given the broken modifier, any untrusted actor) calls `undelegateAmount` with amounts that the validator partially fulfills; the proxy then tries to deposit `totalUndelegated` which may exceed its balance, reverting the whole tx (DoS) or, if it has residual balance from `receive()`, draining that residual to the vault.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on undelegation or loss of residual RON held by the proxy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual balance delta before/after `bulkUndelegate` and deposit only the delta.

hypotheses.title: requestWithdrawal does not verify user has enough shares or allowance
hypotheses.description: `requestWithdrawal` calls `_transfer(msg.sender, address(this), _shares)` which will revert if the user lacks balance, so that is fine. However, it does not check that `_shares > 0`, and more importantly it does not prevent a user from requesting withdrawal in an epoch that has already been finalised (since `withdrawalEpoch` is the current epoch, and finalise increments it, this is mostly safe). The real issue: `_checkUserCanReceiveRon` uses a `call{value:0}` which can be griefed by a contract that reverts on receive, but that only blocks the user themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor against others; the check is self-limiting.
hypotheses.impact: Minimal.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(_shares > 0)`.
